body: Markets · elasticity · journals · merchandising
Semester 1 is **microeconomics**. Semester 2 is **bookkeeping** (personal + business, then merchandising vs service). Grade 12 later adds GDP and depreciation — don’t mix the years.

cards.title: 1 · Market structures
body: Microeconomics looks at one product, one firm, one household — not the whole nation’s GDP.
**Perfect competition** (the textbook’s starting model) needs all of these at once:

cards.title: Many buyers & sellers
body: Nobody is big enough to set the price. Firm is a *price taker*. Its demand curve is a flat line at market P.

cards.title: Homogeneous product
body: Bags of the same grain look alike. No brand loyalty trick.

cards.title: Perfect information
body: Everyone knows the going price. Raise yours and you sell zero.

cards.title: Free entry / exit + mobility
body: Labour and capital can leave a dying use and enter a fat one. No licence wall.

cards.title: Mnemonic — H.I.M.E.
body: *Homogeneous, Information, Many firms, Entry free.* Drop any letter and the market is already “imperfect”.

cards.title: Market
body: **Imperfect markets** (for contrast): monopoly (one seller), oligopoly (few), monopolistic competition (many but branded). Price makers face a downward-sloping demand curve.

cards.title: Left: market sets P. Right: one tiny firm can sell all it wants at that P — horizontal demand.
1.1.1 Market Structure
body: Markets are structured or built up of buyers on one side and sellers on the other side.
The behavior of a seller is influenced by the features (structure) of the market in which he/she sells his/her products and the costs of production.
The major organizational features of markets are called the structure of a market or market structure.
Entry can vary from perfectly free or no barrier to totally blocked or no entry.

cards.title: Demand and supply
body: **Demand:** quantities buyers will take at each price, other things equal. Law: P up → Qd down (usually).
**Supply:** quantities sellers will offer. Law: P up → Qs up.
Move *along* the curve when the good’s own price changes. *Shift* the whole curve when income, tastes, input costs, weather, number of firms, expected future prices change.

cards.title: Trick
body: Price of the good itself = slide on the line. Everything else = new line. Examiners live on that distinction.

cards.title: Worked
cards.problem: Market for sorghum. Drought kills half the crop. What happens to the supply curve and to P?

steps.text: Drought is not “the price of sorghum” — it is a shifter (worse conditions).
Supply shifts left (less offered at every price).
Demand unchanged → new meeting point: higher P, lower Q.

cards.answer: Demand unchanged → new meeting point: higher P, lower Q.

cards.title: 1.2.1 Equilibrium Price and Quantity
body: The interaction of demand and supply determines the equilibrium market price and equilibrium quantity of any good or service.
Equilibrium Price: Equilibrium price is the market price where the quantity demanded for a good or service is exactly equal to the quantity of the good or service supplied.
The equilibrium price is the price at which the quantity of the good or service that buyers want to buy and the quantity sellers want to sell is the same.
The equilibrium market price is Pe, while the equilibrium quantity is Qe.

PED = (%ΔQd) / (%ΔP) (ignore the minus in many school papers)

cards.title: 1.3.1 Elasticity of Demand
body: For some goods and services, a small change in the price affects quantity demanded greatly.
For others, a small change in the price has no appreciable effect on the quantity demanded.
Price elasticity of demand thus measures responsiveness of buyers to the change in the price of the good or service under consideration.
Price elasticity of demand is thus a unitfree measure that is conventionally expressed in terms of positive or absolute value.

cards.title: 1.3.2 Elasticity of Supply
body: Elasticity of supply is the measure of the degree to which quantity supplied responds to changes in one of the variables which affect the quantity supplied.
The interpretation is that an increase in the price of sun eyeglasses by 10 per cent will lead to the increase in the quantity of eyeglasses supplied by 30 per cent.
When price increases from Nakfa 2,000 to Nakfa, 3,000 the percentage change in quantity of maize supplied = (700-400/400) x100 = +75%.
The interpretation is that an increase in the price of maize by10 per cent will increase quantity of maize supplied by 15 per cent.

cards.title: 1.4 Cost of Production
body: The word ‘Cost’ is commonly used in day to day life and is at the centre of many economic decisions made at the individual, household, firm, national and international level.
Accountants tend to be more concerned with the firm’s finances because they have to keep track of assets and liabilities and evaluate the financial performance.
Economic cost is somewhat different from accounting cost and it is related to the opportunity cost concept.
Although opportunity cost is often hidden, it should be taken into account when making decisions.
Sunk cost is an expenditure that has been made and that cannot be recovered.

cards.title: 1.5 Consumer Choice and Demand
body: In general, all individuals face two facts of economic life when they make their choices on consumption of goods and services.
Preferences do not represent actual choices.
In explaining consumer preferences, economists make certain assumptions.

The first assumption is that consumers are able to compare one bundle of goods to other bundle of goods and state either they prefer one to the other or be entirely indifferent between the alternatives.
Other important assumption is that individuals are rational in making decisions and they prefer more than less of the goods and services they consume.

glossary.meaning: Monopoly (one seller), oligopoly (few), monopolistic competition (many but branded).
A market is an institution or a mechanism, through which sellers and buyers interact and engage in the exchange of their goods, services and resources (inputs).
Oligopoly is a market structure where there are a few sellers that produce homogeneous or heterogeneous products.
Compared to a perfect competition, oligopoly is an inefficient market as buyers are charged higher prices.
Each seller has a certain degree of monopoly as it is the only producer of the particular brand or variety of the products.
Monopolistic competition is a market condition in which large numbers of firms (sellers) produce similar but differentiated products.
Oligopoly is a market structure where there are a few sellers that produce homogeneous or heterogeneous products.
Duopoly is a market structure where there are only two sellers of homogenous or differentiated products.
Imperfect competition occurs when there are a number of competing sellers (firms) but the market lacks some or all the features of perfect competition.
Interdependence refers to the degree to which the actions of one firm affect the actions of the others.
Demand is the amount of goods or services consumers are willing and able to purchase at a given price and at a given time.
Perfect market is a theoretical market structure in which there are many buyers and sellers of homogenous products where no single seller or buyer has the power to influence the market price.
Individual demand is the quantity of goods or services demanded by an individual buyer (consumer) at a given price and time.
Market demand is the aggregate or the total amount of quantity demanded by all buyers (consumers).
Demand schedule is a table showing the relationship between the price of a good or service and the quantity of the good or service demanded in a given period of time, other things being equal.
Demand curve is a diagram showing the relationship between the price of a good and the quantity demanded in a given period of time, other things being equal.
Market price is the main determinant of the quantity demanded for goods and services by consumers.
Supply curve is a curve or a graph that shows the amount of goods or services sold/offered at different prices.

tips.text: In a free market, economic decisions are coordinated by market mechanism.
The operation of the market system allows resources to be allocated, and goods and services to be produced and distributed in accordance with the market forces of demand and supply.
Economic decisions have to be made both by consumers and by producers.
Consumers can choose between a large number of goods and services supplied into the market.
For each good, consumers must decide how much they are willing and able to buy from the market.
Producers must decide how much they are going to produce and supply into the market.
Consumers and producers meet each other in the market.
Coordination between the total quantity demanded by consumers and the total quantity supplied by producers is achieved through the interaction of the market supply and demand.
Economists group different market structures into five categories. These categories are perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition, oligopoly and duopoly.
With the exception of perfect competition, all the other market structures are collectively referred to imperfect markets.
Many buyers & sellers: Nobody is big enough to set the price. Firm is a price taker. Its demand curve is a flat line at market P.
Homogeneous product: Bags of the same grain look alike. No brand loyalty trick.
Perfect information: Everyone knows the going price. Raise yours and you sell zero.
Free entry / exit + mobility: Labour and capital can leave a dying use and enter a fat one. No licence wall.

cards.title: 2.1.1 Purchases Journal
body: Asmara Shoes and Clothing Business buys merchandise either in cash or on credit.
A special journal for recording purchases of merchandise on account is called a Purchase Journal.
A merchandising business may buy many items such as merchandise, supplies and fixed assets.
Other assets bought for use in the business rather than for resale are recorded in other appropriate general ledger accounts.

cards.title: Records
body: If you don’t write it down, you don’t know if the shop lived or died. Personal cash book first, then business books.
**Double entry:** every story has two sides. Debit the receiver / the asset that grew / the expense. Credit the giver / the liability that grew / the income.

cards.title: Mnemonic — “DEAD CLIC”
body: *Debit* Expenses, Assets, Drawings. *Credit* Liabilities, Income, Capital.

cards.problem: Bought shelves 4,000 Nfa cash. Sold a service 1,200 Nfa cash.

steps.text: Shelves = asset up → Dr Furniture 4,000; cash down → Cr Cash 4,000.
Service = income → Cr Service revenue 1,200; cash up → Dr Cash 1,200.
Never debit and credit the same idea twice for one event.

cards.answer: Never debit and credit the same idea twice for one event.

cards.title: Merchandising vs service
body: **Service business** sells time/skill (barber, clinic). Income = fees. No stock of goods for resale.
**Merchandising** buys goods and sells them on (dukan, wholesaler). You need a Purchases (or Inventory) account and you calculate:
Sales − Cost of goods sold = Gross profit Gross profit − Expenses = Net profit

cards.title: 2.2.1 Reasons for Cash Payments
body: Whenever merchandise is purchased, the purchases account is debited.
Merchandises are items purchased in order to be sold; while supplies are purchased for use in the business.
As such, accounts payable has its own separate column in the cash payments journal.
Payment of accounts payable is a settlement for merchandise previously purchased on account.

cards.title: 2.2.2 Schedule of Accounts Payable
body: A list of all creditor’s that shows the balance owed to each creditor and the total amount owed to all creditors is called the Schedule of Accounts Payable.
2, Identify the transaction(s) that should be journalized in a cash payments journal. a.
Purchase of equipment on account, for Nakfa.17,000. b.
Purchase of machinery of Nakfa 12,000 for cash. c.

cards.title: 2.3 Sales Journal
body: The sales journal is a book of original entry designed to handle only the sale of merchandise on credit.
A sales journal is sometimes known as a sales book or a sale register.
Charge Customer (Debtor): is a customer to whom a sale on account is made. b.
Creditor: is a person or firm that sells goods or services on credit. c.
Credit term: is the term of payment on the Credit Invoice.

cards.title: 2.4.1 Journalizing Cash Receipts
body: The cash register registers the sales transaction and a cash register slip is printed and handed to the customer.
The cash sales invoice contains a description of the quantity and types of goods bought for cash.
The original is given to the customer and the duplicate remains in the cash sales invoice book and is used to journalize the information to the cash receipts journal.

Step 2: Recording the name of a charge customer (for collection of accounts receivable) or the general ledger account name (for transactions recorded in the sundry account) in the account credited column.

cards.title: 2.4.2 Posting from Cash Receipts Journal
body: As with the sales journal, the subsidiary ledger accounts are posted each day.
To indicate that this has been posted, the accounts receivable control account number (12) is placed under accounts receivable credit column.
On January 1, the owner invested 100,000 in the business and on January. 4, the company borrowed 10,000 from the bank by issuing a loan payable.
At the end of the month the amounts found in the sundry column are posted to their respective general ledger accounts.

cards.title: 2.4.3 Schedule of Accounts Receivable
body: If all posting from the sales journal and cash receipts journal were correctly done, the balance of the controlling account, the accounts receivable account, in the general ledger will be the sum of the balances of the customers; accounts in the accounts receivable ledger.

lessons.title: Recording Miscellaneous Entries in the General Journal

cards.title: 2.5.1 Journalizing Purchases of other Assets except Merchandise on Account
body: Businesses occasionally purchase (acquire) assets other than merchandise such as supplies, delivery equipment etc. on account.
Since the items are not merchandise such acquisitions cannot be recorded in a purchase journal.

cards.title: 2.5.2 Journalizing Sales Returns and Allowance
body: Merchandising businesses usually allow a customer to return goods that are defective or unsatisfactory for a variety of reasons, such as wrong colour, wrong size, wrong style, wrong amounts or inferior quality.
Merchandise physically returned by a buyer is referred to as a sales return.
Perhaps a customer’s reason for wishing to return an item is because of a defect.
If this occurs, the seller and the buyer regard a sale return as a cancellation of a sale.

cards.title: 2.5.3 Journalizing Purchase Returns and Allowance
body: A purchaser may be dissatisfied with the merchandise received because the goods are damaged or defective, of inferior quality, or not in accord with the purchaser’s specifications.
In such cases, the purchaser may return the goods to the supplier for credit if the sale was made on credit or for a cash refund if the purchase was originally for cash.
Alternatively, the purchaser may choose to keep the merchandise if the seller is willing to grant an allowance (deduction) from the purchase price.
The buyer initiates the request for a reduction of the balance due through the issuance of a debit memorandum.

cards.title: 2.6.1 The Worksheet
body: The period-end procedures of adjusting entries, preparing financial statements, and closing the temporary (nominal) accounts are all procedures that a merchandising business must do periodically, just like a service business.
A very helpful accounting tool in completing the period-end procedures is the worksheet.
The worksheet assembles the relationship between the unadjusted trial balance, proposed adjusting entries, and the financial statements in one centre.
The unadjusted trial balance is a list of closing general ledger balances, after all transactions have been posted from the various journals, in their proper normal balance.

cards.title: 2.6.2 Preparing Financial Statements from the Worksheet
body: The worksheet is an efficient device for organizing and summarizing financial data about the operation of a business.
The worksheet is also an efficient means of planning the adjustments to bring the general ledger accounts up to date.
A more effective way of doing this is by means of the financial statements.

Unlike the income statement of a service business which has mainly two sections, revenue section and expenses section, the income statement for a merchandising business has three sections: (1) the revenue section, (2) the cost of goods sold section, and (3) the expenses section.

body: Adjusting Entry for the Beginning Merchandise Inventory In the worksheet, the debit and credit parts of this adjustment are identified by the reference letter (a).
The words Adjusting Entries are written in the middle of the general journal’s Account Title column to explain the entry and all the adjusting entries that follow.
In the worksheet, the debit and credit parts of this adjustment are identified by the reference letter (b).
Adjusting Entry for Supplies In the worksheet, the debit and credit parts of this adjustment are identified by the reference letter (c).

cards.title: 2.7.2 Closing Entries
body: Closing the temporary accounts is necessary to prepare the general ledger of the business for the next fiscal period.
Only the owner’s drawing account is taken from the worksheet balance sheet columns.
To close accounts with credit normal balance: This consists of all revenue accounts and all contra-purchase accounts.
To close accounts with debit normal balance: This consists of all expense accounts, purchase accounts including freight-in, and all contra-sales accounts.

cards.title: 2.7.3 Posting the Adjusting and Closing Entries to the General Ledger
body: The general ledger accounts will not be updated and will not be ready for the next fiscal year unless all the adjusting and closing entries are posted to the accounts affected.

cards.title: 2.7.4 Post-Closing Trial Balance
body: Accounts with zero balances are not listed.

tips.text: A merchandising business is a business that buys and sells merchandise to earn profit.
A merchandising business that purchases and sells directly to consumers are retailers, and those that sell to retailers in large quantities are known as wholesalers.
Merchandising businesses uses special journals to record the most frequent transactions in a business.

Special Journals are designed to facilitate the process of journalizing and posting transactions. There are four types of special journals, namely, purchase journal, cash payments journal, sales journal and cash receipt journals.
Transactions that are not recorded in these special journals are recorded in a general journal.
The special journal which is used for recording only the purchase of merchandise on credit is called a Purchase Journal.
The source document for recording a transaction in a purchase journal is a Credit Purchase invoice.
Every purchase of merchandise on accounts results in a debit to the purchase account and a credit to the accounts payable account.
Purchase journal entries are posted to both accounts payable account in the general ledger and accounts payable accounts in subsidiary ledgers.
The total of the purchases journal is posted to the two general ledger accounts, debit to purchases and credit to accounts payable at the end of the month.

pairs.b: The goods that a merchandising business buys for resale to customers are called Merchandises.

items.text: Merchandising Business: The goods that a merchandising business buys for resale to customers are called Merchandises.
Credit Purchase Invoice: A credit purchase invoice is an external sources document received when a merchandising business buys goods on credit from sellers.
items.why: That describes Purchase. Credit Purchase Invoice: A credit purchase invoice is an external sources document received when a merchandising business buys goods on credit from sellers.

items.text: Merchandise: Merchandise Inventory, is the only new thing included in the Balance Sheet of a Merchandising business.
Control Account: Likewise, an Accounts Payable Controlling Account is a summary account showing the total amount owed to various suppliers (creditors).
items.why: That describes Accounts Payable. Control Account: A Control Account is an account in the general ledger that shows the total balance of all the subsidiary accounts related to it.

items.text: Purchase: A credit purchase invoice is an external sources document received when a merchandising business buys goods on credit from sellers.
Freight Out: If the agreement is F.O.B shipping point, then it means that the seller agrees to pay for transportation costs up to the shipping point.
items.why: That describes F.O.B Shipping Point. Freight Out: Except freight out, all other operating expenses are the same with the expenses of a service company.

items.text: Accounts Payable: Likewise, an Accounts Payable Controlling Account is a summary account showing the total amount owed to various suppliers (creditors).
Sales Journal: Payment of accounts payable is a settlement for merchandise previously purchased on account.
items.why: That describes Payment of accounts payable. Sales Journal: The sales journal is a book of original entry designed to handle only the sale of merchandise on credit.
